item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating persistent interests from current intent, then learning their interaction. [MSMT-LSI (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5) combines separate long- and short-term attention networks with temporal embeddings. [Hierarchical long/short-term modeling (online 2025)](https://journal.hep.com.cn/fcs/EN/10.1007/s11704-025-41181-y) uses dynamic routing to extract multiple long-term preference vectors, short-term self-attention, and similarity-based matching to retrieve persistent interests relevant to current behavior. [HM4SR (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14269) introduces separate interest-filtering and temporal MoE stages, incorporating explicit timestamps. Its multimodal inputs and category-supervision objective exceed this benchmark’s available data, so direct reproduction would require adaptation.\n\n[Mixture of Sequence (WWW 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20858) directly addresses recurring interests: sessions can shift themes abruptly, while earlier themes may return. It routes sessions into coherent thematic subsequences and combines global, short-term, and theme-specific experts. A plausible benchmark adaptation, inferred from these designs, is a small recent-intent encoder plus several historical interest slots, with a learned gate conditioned on recent/history agreement and observed time gaps. Older interactions could regain weight through relevance to current intent rather than receive uniform decay. These papers motivate the architecture; they do not establish gains on the pinned RecHarness evaluation. Compare against SASRec and fixed-recency pooling through ablations of multiple interests, temporal inputs, and adaptive gating, selecting by macro validation HR@10."}
